critical_action: Hemoglobin <7.0 g/dL: evaluate for transfusion (target >8 in cardiac patients, >7 in stable patients); identify and treat underlying cause. Hemoglobin >20 g/dL: evaluate for polycythemia vera (JAK2 V617F), secondary polycythemia (hypoxia, EPO-secreting tumor); consider phlebotomy.
high_indicates: Secondary polycythemia (COPD, high altitude, EPO abuse)
content: Hemoglobin (Hgb) is the primary component of red blood cells responsible for oxygen transport. It is measured as part of the complete blood count (CBC) and is the key parameter for diagnosing and classifying anemia. Normal values differ by sex: 13.5-17.5 g/dL for adult males, 12.0-15.5 g/dL for adult females, reflecting differences in androgen-driven erythropoiesis and menstrual losses. Critical low is below 7.0 g/dL — at this threshold, most patients are symptomatic with fatigue, dyspnea on exertion, tachycardia, and possibly angina. Transfusion is generally indicated below 7.0 g/dL in stable patients (restrictive strategy — TRICC trial) or below 8.0 g/dL in patients with active cardiac disease or acute coronary syndrome. Low hemoglobin causes include iron deficiency (most common worldwide — look for microcytic MCV and low ferritin), vitamin B12 or folate deficiency (macrocytic anemia), anemia of chronic disease (normocytic, low reticulocyte index), hemolytic anemia (elevated LDH, low haptoglobin, elevated reticulocyte count), aplastic anemia (pancytopenia), and CKD (EPO deficiency). The reticulocyte count differentiates hypoproliferative (low reticulocytes) from hyperproliferative (high reticulocytes) causes. Hemoglobin above 17.5 g/dL in men or 15.5 g/dL in women is erythrocytosis — causes include polycythemia vera (JAK2 mutation), secondary erythrocytosis from chronic hypoxia (COPD, sleep apnea, high altitude), and EPO-secreting tumors (renal cell carcinoma). Always interpret hemoglobin in the clinical context: a hemoglobin of 9.0 g/dL in a young patient with iron deficiency responding to supplementation is managed differently from the same level in a patient with AML and bone marrow failure.

critical_high: >120 fL (severe macrocytosis)
critical_action: MCV <60 fL with anemia: urgent evaluation for severe iron deficiency, thalassemia, or lead poisoning. MCV >120 fL: evaluate for B12/folate deficiency or bone marrow pathology; check blood smear for hypersegmented neutrophils (megaloblastic anemia marker).
content: MCV (Mean Corpuscular Volume) measures the average size of red blood cells and is essential for classifying anemia by morphology, which directly guides the diagnostic workup. The normal MCV is 80-100 fL. Microcytic anemia (MCV <80 fL) is caused by conditions impairing hemoglobin synthesis: iron deficiency (most common — low ferritin, high TIBC, low serum iron), thalassemia (normal or elevated ferritin, abnormal hemoglobin electrophoresis), anemia of chronic disease (usually normocytic but can be mildly microcytic), lead poisoning (basophilic stippling on smear), and sideroblastic anemia (ring sideroblasts on bone marrow). Macrocytic anemia (MCV >100 fL) is caused by defects in DNA synthesis or maturation: vitamin B12 deficiency (pernicious anemia from anti-intrinsic factor antibodies, strict vegan diet, gastrectomy), folate deficiency (malnutrition, pregnancy, alcohol, methotrexate, trimethoprim), alcohol use disorder (direct toxic effect on erythropoiesis), hypothyroidism, liver disease, and medications (hydroxyurea, zidovudine, methotrexate). Megaloblastic anemia from B12 or folate deficiency is characterized by hypersegmented neutrophils (>5 lobes or ≥1 neutrophil with ≥6 lobes) on peripheral smear — a pathognomonic finding. The RDW (red cell distribution width) helps distinguish iron deficiency (elevated RDW with low MCV) from thalassemia trait (normal or only mildly elevated RDW with low MCV — Mentzer index <13 suggests thalassemia). Always pair MCV with clinical context, ferritin, B12, folate, and peripheral smear for complete anemia characterization.

critical_high: >1000 ng/mL (hemochromatosis or hyperferritinemia syndrome workup required)
critical_action: Ferritin <12: initiate iron replacement therapy (oral ferrous sulfate first-line; IV iron if GI intolerance or malabsorption). Ferritin >1000: consider hemochromatosis (HFE gene testing, liver biopsy if transferrin saturation >45%), still disease, hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH), or acute liver failure.
low_indicates: Iron deficiency anemia (most specific test for iron deficiency)
Iron-restricted erythropoiesis before overt anemia develops
content: Ferritin is the intracellular iron storage protein and the single most useful laboratory test for diagnosing iron deficiency. Ferritin reflects total body iron stores — a low ferritin is virtually diagnostic of iron deficiency, making it the most specific test for this condition. The threshold for iron deficiency is ferritin below 30 ng/mL in most guidelines (below 12 ng/mL is classic deficiency, 12-30 ng/mL is probable deficiency especially if microcytic or symptomatic anemia is present). The critical caveat is that ferritin is an acute-phase reactant — inflammatory conditions, infection, liver disease, malignancy, and Still disease can falsely elevate ferritin into the normal or even high range despite true iron deficiency. In a patient with suspected iron deficiency and ferritin 50-100 ng/mL in the setting of inflammation, additional tests (transferrin saturation, serum iron, reticulocyte hemoglobin content) help distinguish iron-restricted erythropoiesis from adequate iron stores. Markedly elevated ferritin above 1000 ng/mL warrants evaluation for hemochromatosis (HFE C282Y/H63D mutation, transferrin saturation >45%), acute liver necrosis (massive hepatocyte ferritin release), hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH — fever, hepatosplenomegaly, cytopenias, very high ferritin >10,000, hypertriglyceridemia), and adult-onset Still disease (quotidian fever, salmon-colored rash, arthritis, ferritin often >10,000). In men and postmenopausal women, iron deficiency anemia always requires endoscopic evaluation to exclude gastrointestinal malignancy as the source of blood loss. Ferritin below 100 ng/mL can cause symptoms of iron deficiency (fatigue, cognitive impairment, restless legs) even without anemia — a condition known as iron deficiency without anemia that also benefits from supplementation.

critical_high: >30,000 cells/µL (possible leukemia or severe infection/leukemoid reaction)
critical_action: WBC <500 neutrophils (ANC): reverse isolation precautions; empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics if febrile (cefepime or piperacillin-tazobactam); G-CSF consideration; hematology consult. WBC >30,000: evaluate for leukemia (blood smear, flow cytometry), severe infection/sepsis (procalcitonin, cultures), or leukemoid reaction.
content: The white blood cell (WBC) count measures the total circulating leukocytes and, with the differential, identifies which cell lines are abnormal to guide diagnosis. Normal range is 4,500-11,000 cells/µL. The absolute neutrophil count (ANC) is calculated from the WBC differential: ANC = WBC × (% neutrophils + % bands). An ANC below 1,500 is neutropenia, below 1,000 is moderate neutropenia, and below 500 is severe neutropenia with high infection risk requiring empiric antibiotics and febrile neutropenia protocols. Leukocytosis above 11,000 is most commonly due to bacterial infection, physiological stress responses (corticosteroids shift neutrophils from marginated to circulating pool), or smoking-related chronic inflammation. Very high WBC above 30,000 raises concern for leukemia — acute leukemia presents with blasts on peripheral smear, cytopenias, and constitutional symptoms; chronic leukemias (CML, CLL) have more mature cell populations and often present incidentally. A leukemoid reaction is a reactive (benign) WBC rise above 50,000 in response to severe infection, hemolysis, or malignancy — distinguished from CML by absence of BCR-ABL translocation and elevated leukocyte alkaline phosphatase. Leukopenia below 4,500 occurs with viral infections (lymphopenia in COVID-19, influenza, HIV), drug toxicity (chemotherapy, clozapine, methimazole), autoimmune disease (SLE neutropenia), and bone marrow failure. Bandemia (elevated band neutrophils, the 'left shift') indicates immature granulocyte release in response to acute bacterial infection or stress, supporting the clinical diagnosis of sepsis even when the total WBC is not dramatically elevated.

critical_high: >1,000,000 (thrombocytosis — thrombosis and paradoxical bleeding risk)
critical_action: Platelets <20,000: transfuse platelets (1 platelet pack raises count ~5,000-10,000); assess for ITP (treat with IVIG and/or steroids), TTP (PLASMA EXCHANGE — do NOT transfuse platelets in TTP/HUS), HIT (stop heparin immediately). Platelets >1,000,000: evaluate for essential thrombocythemia (JAK2, CALR mutations); risk-stratify for cytoreduction (hydroxyurea) if high-risk.
high_indicates: Reactive thrombocytosis (infection, iron deficiency, post-splenectomy, inflammation)
content: Platelet count reflects the circulating thrombocytes responsible for primary hemostasis. Normal range is 150,000-400,000 cells/µL. Thrombocytopenia (count below 150,000) is classified by mechanism: decreased production (bone marrow failure from aplastic anemia, leukemia, chemotherapy, B12/folate deficiency), increased destruction (immune — ITP, TTP, HIT; non-immune — DIC, mechanical heart valves, sepsis), or sequestration (splenomegaly causing hypersplenism). Critical clinical distinctions: In ITP (immune thrombocytopenic purpura), isolated thrombocytopenia with normal smear and no other cell line involvement is treated with steroids and/or IVIG. In TTP (thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura), thrombocytopenia occurs with microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (schistocytes, elevated LDH, low haptoglobin), neurological changes, fever, and renal dysfunction — plasma exchange (plasmapheresis) is life-saving and platelet transfusion is contraindicated (may worsen thrombosis). Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) occurs 5-10 days after heparin exposure with platelet drop >50% from baseline; the paradox is thrombosis, not bleeding — stop all heparin immediately and use argatroban or bivalirudin. DIC shows thrombocytopenia with prolonged PT/INR, low fibrinogen, and elevated D-dimer. A platelet count below 50,000 is a contraindication to most invasive procedures; below 20,000 carries risk of spontaneous mucosal or intracranial bleeding. Thrombocytosis above 600,000 requires evaluation for essential thrombocythemia (JAK2 V617F or CALR mutation) versus reactive thrombocytosis (iron deficiency, infection, post-splenectomy, inflammatory disease).

critical_high: >155 mEq/L (altered consciousness); >160 mEq/L (lethal risk)
critical_action: Hyponatremia <125: determine onset (acute vs. chronic >48h), symptoms, and volume status. Acute symptomatic: 3% NaCl 1-2 mL/kg/hr; raise Na no faster than 1-2 mEq/L/hr until symptoms resolve, then slow to <8-10 mEq/L/24h (prevent osmotic demyelination syndrome). Hypernatremia >155: calculate free water deficit; replace with hypotonic fluids at rate not exceeding 10-12 mEq/L/24h correction.
high_indicates: Inadequate free water intake (impaired thirst in elderly or neurologically impaired)
low_indicates: Hyponatremia: SIADH (most common in hospitalized patients)
content: Serum sodium is the primary determinant of serum osmolality and extracellular fluid tonicity, making it a fundamental electrolyte in clinical assessment. Normal range is 136-145 mEq/L. Hyponatremia (Na <136 mEq/L) is the most common electrolyte disorder in hospitalized patients and requires systematic evaluation of volume status, serum osmolality, and urine indices. Step 1: check serum osmolality — if low (hypotonic), proceed with evaluation; if normal (isotonic — pseudohyponatremia from hyperproteinemia or hyperlipidemia) or high (hypertonic — hyperglycemia, mannitol), address the underlying cause. Step 2: assess volume status. Hypovolemic hyponatremia (dehydration with free water replacement): urine sodium <20 suggests extra-renal losses (GI, sweating); urine sodium >20 suggests renal losses (diuretics, cerebral salt wasting). Euvolemic hyponatremia: most commonly SIADH (urine Na >40, urine osmolality >300, no edema, no dehydration) — causes include CNS disease, pulmonary disease, medications (SSRIs, carbamazepine, cyclophosphamide, NSAIDs), pain, and surgery. Hypervolemic hyponatremia: heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome (dilutional — low urine sodium as kidneys retain sodium). The most feared complication of correction is osmotic demyelination syndrome (ODS, formerly central pontine myelinolysis) from too-rapid correction of chronic hyponatremia — maximum correction rate is 8-10 mEq/L per 24 hours in chronic hyponatremia. Acute symptomatic hyponatremia (seizures, coma) requires rapid correction with 3% hypertonic saline until symptoms resolve. Hypernatremia (Na >145) is always due to free water deficit — causes include diabetes insipidus, excessive sweating, osmotic diuresis, or inadequate intake in impaired-thirst patients.

critical_low: <3.0 mEq/L (arrhythmia risk); <2.5 mEq/L (life-threatening paralysis and arrhythmia)
critical_high: >5.5 mEq/L (cardiac monitoring required); >6.5 mEq/L (life-threatening)
critical_action: Hypokalemia <3.0: oral or IV KCl replacement; monitor ECG (flattened T-waves, U waves, prolonged QU); co-replete magnesium (hypokalemia is refractory without Mg). Hyperkalemia >6.0 or with ECG changes: calcium gluconate 1g IV immediately; insulin 10 units + D50; albuterol 10-20mg nebulized; sodium bicarbonate if acidotic; furosemide/kayexalate; emergent dialysis if severe.
high_indicates: Hypoaldosteronism (Addison disease, ACE inhibitor/ARB + K-sparing diuretic)
related_tests: ECG (peaked T-waves in hyperkalemia; U-waves in hypokalemia)
content: Serum potassium is the most clinically critical electrolyte due to its direct effects on cardiac membrane excitability. Normal range is 3.5-5.0 mEq/L. Both hyperkalemia and hypokalemia can cause fatal arrhythmias and require prompt ECG evaluation when values are critical. Hyperkalemia (K+ >5.0) is treated in a stepwise approach based on severity and ECG changes: any ECG changes (peaked T-waves, prolonged PR, widened QRS, sine wave pattern, ventricular fibrillation) mandate immediate calcium gluconate 1g IV over 2-3 minutes to stabilize the cardiac membrane. Insulin-glucose (10 units regular insulin IV + 25g dextrose) shifts K+ intracellularly within 15-30 minutes, as does nebulized albuterol 10-20mg. Sodium bicarbonate is effective in acidotic patients. These measures are temporary — definitive removal requires loop diuretics, sodium polystyrene sulfonate (kayexalate), patiromer, or dialysis for severe or refractory cases. The most common cause of severe hyperkalemia in the outpatient setting is the combination of CKD with ACE inhibitors/ARBs plus potassium-sparing diuretics or NSAIDs. Always rule out pseudohyperkalemia (hemolyzed sample, difficult venipuncture, tourniquet-induced) before treating. Hypokalemia (K+ <3.5) causes muscle weakness, fatigue, constipation, and at severe levels (<2.5) paralysis and ventricular arrhythmias. ECG changes include flattened T-waves, prominent U-waves, and prolonged QU interval. Oral potassium chloride is preferred for mild-moderate cases; IV replacement is used for severe or symptomatic hypokalemia. Magnesium depletion causes refractory hypokalemia — always check and replete magnesium concurrently. In digoxin-treated patients, hypokalemia is particularly dangerous as it enhances digoxin's inhibition of Na+/K+-ATPase, precipitating digoxin toxicity.

critical_low: Not clinically significant (low creatinine indicates low muscle mass)
critical_high: >4.0 mg/dL (AKI or severe CKD, consider dialysis evaluation)
critical_action: Creatinine >4.0 or rising rapidly (>0.5 mg/dL in 24-48h = AKI): stop nephrotoxic drugs (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, contrast); assess volume status; check urinalysis, urine electrolytes (FENa); renal ultrasound (obstruction); nephrology consult. Creatinine >10 or symptomatic uremia: initiate dialysis discussion.
high_indicates: Medications that block tubular secretion (trimethoprim, cimetidine)
content: Serum creatinine is a metabolic waste product of muscle creatine phosphate turnover and is the standard biomarker for assessing kidney function. It is used to calculate eGFR (estimated glomerular filtration rate) using the CKD-EPI or MDRD equation, which accounts for age, sex, and race. A critical limitation: creatinine is a late marker of kidney injury — the serum creatinine does not rise above the normal range until approximately 50% of kidney function is lost. In elderly or malnourished patients with low muscle mass, creatinine can remain within the normal range despite significantly impaired GFR (a patient with a creatinine of 1.0 mg/dL who is elderly and frail may have an eGFR of only 40-50 mL/min). Acute kidney injury (AKI) is defined by a creatinine rise of ≥0.3 mg/dL within 48 hours or ≥1.5 times baseline within 7 days. AKI is classified as pre-renal (hypovolemia, reduced perfusion — BUN:Cr ratio >20:1, FENa <1%), intrinsic renal (acute tubular necrosis most common — FENa >2%, muddy brown casts on urinalysis; also glomerulonephritis, interstitial nephritis), or post-renal (obstruction — hydronephrosis on ultrasound, elevated post-void residual). CKD staging by eGFR: G1 (≥90), G2 (60-89), G3a (45-59), G3b (30-44), G4 (15-29), G5 (<15). Dose adjustment of renally-cleared medications is essential in CKD to prevent drug toxicity. The combination of an NSAID, ACE inhibitor/ARB, and diuretic (the triple whammy) in a dehydrated patient is a common cause of hospital-acquired AKI. Cystatin C is an alternative GFR marker not affected by muscle mass, useful in confirming renal function in patients where creatinine may be misleading.

critical_high: >50 mg/dL (uremia risk); >100 mg/dL (severe renal failure)
critical_action: BUN >50 with symptoms of uremia (nausea, encephalopathy, pericarditis, platelet dysfunction): nephrology consultation for dialysis evaluation. BUN <5 with jaundice or encephalopathy: evaluate for acute liver failure (LFTs, INR, ammonia).
high_indicates: Upper GI bleeding (blood protein digested to urea)
content: Blood urea nitrogen (BUN) measures the nitrogen component of urea, the primary end-product of protein catabolism synthesized in the liver from ammonia. BUN is used alongside creatinine to assess renal function and guide differential diagnosis of elevated creatinine. The BUN:creatinine ratio is a key diagnostic tool: a ratio above 20:1 suggests pre-renal azotemia (reduced renal perfusion from dehydration, heart failure, or hypovolemia) or upper gastrointestinal bleeding (blood protein is digested and absorbed as nitrogen, raising BUN without increasing creatinine proportionally). A ratio below 10-15:1 with elevated creatinine suggests intrinsic renal disease (acute tubular necrosis, glomerulonephritis). Normal BUN is 7-20 mg/dL. High protein intake, catabolic states (sepsis, trauma, corticosteroid therapy), and tetracyclines also raise BUN independently of renal function. Low BUN below 5 mg/dL is an important marker of severe hepatic synthetic failure — the liver is unable to synthesize urea from ammonia, which then accumulates causing hepatic encephalopathy. In cirrhosis, low BUN combined with elevated serum ammonia and encephalopathic symptoms confirms hepatic failure. BUN is also useful for monitoring dialysis adequacy (Kt/V calculation, urea reduction ratio). In rhabdomyolysis, BUN rises disproportionately due to release of myoglobin and muscle creatine, contributing to AKI through tubular obstruction. Uremia — the symptomatic syndrome of renal failure — presents with nausea, vomiting, anorexia, encephalopathy, pericarditis, platelet dysfunction (uremic platelet dysfunction), and pruritus when BUN is persistently elevated above 50-100 mg/dL, representing an indication for dialysis initiation.

critical_high: >500 mg/dL (DKA or HHS risk)
critical_action: Glucose <50: conscious patient — oral glucose 15-20g (juice, glucose tablets); unconscious — IV dextrose (D50 25mL bolus) or glucagon 1mg IM. Glucose >400 with symptoms: check ketones and pH for DKA (anion gap metabolic acidosis, ketones) vs HHS (serum osmolality >320, minimal ketones); initiate insulin protocol.
specimen: Serum or plasma (fasting — 8 hours no caloric intake)
content: Fasting serum glucose is the primary screening and diagnostic test for diabetes mellitus and its precursors. A fasting glucose of 70-99 mg/dL is normal; 100-125 mg/dL is prediabetes (impaired fasting glucose); 126 mg/dL or above on two separate occasions confirms diabetes mellitus. A random glucose above 200 mg/dL with classic symptoms (polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss) is also diagnostic. Critically elevated glucose above 400 mg/dL in a known or new diabetic should prompt evaluation for DKA versus HHS. DKA is characterized by glucose typically 250-800 mg/dL, anion gap metabolic acidosis (pH <7.35, bicarb <18, anion gap >12), and ketonemia/ketonuria — occurs in Type 1 DM and sometimes Type 2, often triggered by infection, insulin omission, or acute illness. HHS (hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state) presents with glucose typically above 600 mg/dL, serum osmolality above 320 mOsm/kg, mild or no ketosis, and severe dehydration — predominantly in Type 2 DM with impaired thirst. Treatment priorities differ: DKA requires insulin infusion (after potassium is above 3.5), aggressive IV fluids, and electrolyte replacement; HHS requires primarily aggressive fluid replacement and slower glucose correction. Critical hypoglycemia below 50 mg/dL causes adrenergic symptoms (diaphoresis, tremor, tachycardia) and neuroglycopenic symptoms (confusion, seizure, coma). The rule of 15 for conscious patients: 15g of fast-acting carbohydrates, recheck in 15 minutes. Stress hyperglycemia (glucose 140-180 mg/dL in ICU) worsens outcomes and is treated with insulin infusion targeting 140-180 mg/dL (NICE-SUGAR trial — tighter targets increase hypoglycemia risk).

critical_low: <4.0% (suggests hemolytic anemia or EPO use falsely lowering HbA1c)
critical_high: >14% (dangerously poor glycemic control — DKA or HHS risk imminent)
critical_action: HbA1c >10%: intensify diabetes management (add insulin if not on it, or intensify regimen); evaluate for complications (retinopathy, nephropathy, neuropathy, cardiovascular disease); patient education reinforcement; rule out DKA if symptomatic. HbA1c <5.7% in a known diabetic on medication: evaluate for overtreatment (reduce insulin/sulfonylurea).
high_indicates: Infection or other stress increasing glucose
low_indicates: Hemolytic anemia (shortened RBC lifespan — falsely low HbA1c despite high glucose)
Blood transfusion (replaces glycated cells with donor cells)
EPO use (newly made RBCs not yet glycated)
related_tests: Fructosamine (shorter 2-3 week window, useful when HbA1c unreliable)
specimen: Whole blood (EDTA tube) — no fasting required
content: HbA1c (glycated hemoglobin) measures the percentage of hemoglobin that has been irreversibly glycated, reflecting average blood glucose over the preceding 2-3 months (the lifespan of a red blood cell). It is the gold-standard measure of long-term glycemic control and a diagnostic criterion for diabetes mellitus (≥6.5% on two occasions, or once with confirmatory fasting glucose or OGTT). The ADA 2024 glycemic targets for most adults with Type 2 DM is HbA1c below 7% — more stringent targets below 6.5% may be appropriate for younger patients with short disease duration and no hypoglycemia risk; less stringent targets of 7.5-8% are appropriate for elderly, frail, or hypoglycemia-prone patients. Each 1% reduction in HbA1c is associated with approximately 20-30% reduction in microvascular complications (retinopathy, nephropathy, neuropathy) — the foundation of intensive diabetes management. False conditions affecting HbA1c: hemolytic anemia, sickle cell disease, and other hemoglobinopathies shorten RBC lifespan and falsely lower HbA1c despite poor glucose control — fructosamine (2-3 week window) or continuous glucose monitoring should be used instead. Iron deficiency anemia can falsely elevate HbA1c. Blood transfusions introduce donor non-glycated hemoglobin, falsely lowering results. Fasting is not required for HbA1c measurement, making it more convenient than fasting glucose. HbA1c monitoring frequency: every 3 months when uncontrolled or after medication changes, every 6 months when at goal and stable.

critical_high: >5x URL (upper reference limit) strongly suggests myocardial injury; rising pattern (delta ≥3 ng/L at 1 hour or ≥6 ng/L at 3 hours) confirms acute MI
critical_action: Troponin elevated above 99th percentile with rising/falling pattern plus symptoms: activate ACS protocol — ECG, aspirin 325mg, cardiology consult. Stable elevation without rise/fall pattern: evaluate for non-ACS myocardial injury (troponinemia from PE, myocarditis, sepsis, heart failure, renal failure).
high_indicates: Chronic kidney disease (reduced clearance — baseline elevation)
low_indicates: Normal finding — absence of myocardial injury
Very early in MI course (hsTnI detectable within 1 hour of symptom onset)
specimen: Serum or plasma (EDTA or lithium heparin)
content: High-sensitivity troponin I (hsTnI) is the most sensitive and specific biomarker for myocardial cell injury, enabling earlier and more accurate diagnosis of acute myocardial infarction. The key principle is the delta troponin (serial measurement): a single elevated troponin is insufficient for MI diagnosis — the pattern of rise and fall is critical. The ESC 0/1-hour algorithm uses hsTnI at presentation and 1 hour: a value above the assay's 99th percentile URL with a delta rise above 6 ng/L at 1 hour or above 12 ng/L absolute at 1 hour confirms acute MI; a very low absolute value (<5 ng/L) with minimal change rules out MI in 98% of patients. The 0/3-hour algorithm is an alternative with equivalent diagnostic accuracy. Importantly, troponin is elevated in many non-ACS conditions (type 2 myocardial injury) — PE (right ventricular strain), myocarditis, sepsis, decompensated heart failure, hypertensive emergency, Takotsubo cardiomyopathy, and CKD (reduced clearance causing chronic baseline elevation). The distinction is critical: in ACS (type 1 MI from plaque rupture and coronary thrombosis), the pattern shows acute rise and fall with ischemic symptoms and ECG changes; in type 2 MI (supply-demand mismatch from tachycardia, hypotension, anemia), troponin rises with an identifiable precipitant. CK-MB is less sensitive but useful for detecting reinfarction (returns to baseline faster than troponin). Point-of-care hsTnI devices now enable rapid decision-making in the ED. Women have lower 99th percentile thresholds than men — using sex-specific cutoffs improves diagnostic accuracy in female patients.

normal_range_pediatric: Age-specific reference ranges; generally BNP <50 pg/mL
critical_low: Very low BNP (<35 or NT-proBNP <125) essentially rules out heart failure as cause of dyspnea (NPV >95%)
critical_high: BNP >500 or NT-proBNP >2000: high likelihood of decompensated heart failure requiring aggressive diuresis
critical_action: BNP >500 with dyspnea, edema, elevated JVP: diagnose decompensated heart failure; IV furosemide (2.5x home oral dose), strict I/O monitoring, daily weights. NT-proBNP trending up despite therapy: reassess diuretic dose, fluid restriction compliance, and consider cardiology consult.
high_indicates: Acute decompensated heart failure (most important use)
low_indicates: Effectively rules out heart failure as cause of dyspnea when below 100 pg/mL (BNP) or 300 pg/mL (NT-proBNP)
Obesity (lower BNP levels despite heart failure — less reliable)
Flash pulmonary edema early (may not rise yet)
specimen: Serum (BNP — EDTA plasma) or plasma (NT-proBNP — serum or EDTA plasma)
content: B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) and its biologically inactive N-terminal fragment (NT-proBNP) are neurohormones released from ventricular cardiomyocytes in response to increased wall stress from volume overload or pressure overload. They are the primary biomarkers for diagnosing and monitoring heart failure. In the dyspneic patient, BNP below 100 pg/mL or NT-proBNP below 300 pg/mL essentially rules out heart failure (negative predictive value above 95%), while elevated values confirm it and guide treatment intensity. The BREATHING-NOT-PROPERLY trial established BNP as superior to clinical judgment alone for diagnosing acute heart failure in the ED. NT-proBNP has age-adjusted cutoffs: below 125 pg/mL for age under 75, below 450 pg/mL for age 75 and older, reflecting reduced renal clearance in elderly patients. Elevated BNP/NT-proBNP correlates with prognosis — higher levels predict 30-day and 90-day mortality and rehospitalization. Serial measurements guide treatment: BNP that fails to decrease with aggressive diuresis by 30-50% during hospitalization predicts adverse in-hospital outcomes. BNP is not perfectly specific for heart failure — elevated values also occur in pulmonary embolism (right ventricular strain), pulmonary hypertension, myocarditis, and CKD (reduced clearance). Conversely, obesity is associated with lower BNP levels despite heart failure (adipocytes clear BNP) — morbidly obese patients may have less BNP elevation than expected, requiring adjusted interpretation thresholds. BNP-guided discharge planning: targeting BNP below 250 pg/mL before discharge reduces 30-day readmission. For monitoring, NT-proBNP >1000 pg/mL at discharge is associated with high 90-day event rates.

units: µg/mL FEU (fibrinogen equivalent units) or ng/mL
normal_range_adult_male: <0.50 µg/mL FEU (assay-dependent; some report in ng/mL: <500 ng/mL)
critical_high: >4.0 µg/mL FEU (high clinical probability of PE or DVT)
critical_action: D-dimer elevated with clinical suspicion for PE or DVT: proceed to CT pulmonary angiography (CTPA) or venous ultrasound. Age-adjusted D-dimer (age x 10 µg/L for patients >50 years) increases specificity. D-dimer >5 times upper limit with fever, organ failure, and thrombocytopenia: evaluate for DIC (fibrinogen, PT/INR, platelet count, peripheral smear).
low_indicates: Normal fibrinolysis — effectively rules out venous thromboembolism when below threshold in low-to-intermediate pretest probability (NPV >95%)
Not useful for ruling OUT PE/DVT in high pretest probability
content: D-dimer is a fibrin degradation product generated when cross-linked fibrin is broken down by plasmin. It is produced whenever thrombus forms and is lysed, making it highly sensitive (but poorly specific) for venous thromboembolism and other coagulation-activation states. In clinical practice, D-dimer is primarily used as a rule-out test: a negative D-dimer (below the assay cutoff) combined with low or intermediate clinical pretest probability (Wells score for PE or DVT) effectively excludes venous thromboembolism without imaging, reducing the need for radiation and contrast exposure. The negative predictive value is above 95% in this clinical context. However, D-dimer is not a rule-in test — a positive result requires imaging confirmation because D-dimer is elevated in many non-thrombotic conditions including recent surgery, trauma, pregnancy, sepsis, malignancy, liver disease, and simply increasing age. The age-adjusted D-dimer threshold (patient age × 10 ng/mL for patients over 50 years) significantly improves specificity without compromising sensitivity, reducing unnecessary CTPAs in elderly patients. In suspected DIC, markedly elevated D-dimer (often >10 times normal) combined with falling fibrinogen, prolonged PT/INR, thrombocytopenia, and schistocytes on blood smear confirms the diagnosis. DIC is treated by addressing the underlying cause (sepsis, obstetric emergency, malignancy) with supportive blood product replacement (FFP, platelets, cryoprecipitate for fibrinogen). D-dimer in aortic dissection can be markedly elevated (above 500 ng/mL suggests dissection in high pretest probability patients). During pregnancy, D-dimer rises progressively in each trimester — trimester-adjusted cutoffs should be applied.

test_name: PT / INR (Prothrombin Time / International Normalized Ratio)
critical_high: INR >5.0 (major bleeding risk); INR >3.5 in non-anticoagulated patient (suggests severe coagulopathy)
critical_action: INR >5.0 with active bleeding: 4-factor PCC (Kcentra) 25-50 units/kg IV plus vitamin K 10mg IV for immediate reversal; fresh frozen plasma 2-4 units if PCC unavailable. INR >3.5 without bleeding in warfarin patient: hold warfarin, give vitamin K 2.5-5mg PO; recheck in 24-48h. Elevated INR in non-anticoagulated patient: evaluate for liver failure (LFTs, ammonia, albumin), DIC, factor deficiency.
high_indicates: Liver disease / hepatic failure (impaired factor synthesis)
low_indicates: Vitamin K supplementation or dietary excess (green leafy vegetables)
Not clinically significant when below normal
specimen: Plasma (citrate tube — blue top); must be filled to exact volume
content: Prothrombin time (PT) and its standardized form, the INR (International Normalized Ratio), measure the extrinsic and common coagulation pathway (factors VII, X, V, II, and fibrinogen). INR standardizes PT results across different laboratory reagents (thromboplastins), enabling consistent interpretation regardless of the testing facility — essential for monitoring warfarin therapy. Therapeutic INR targets: 2.0-3.0 for most indications (atrial fibrillation, DVT/PE, bioprosthetic valves), 2.5-3.5 for mechanical mitral valves. The key clinical uses of INR: monitoring warfarin therapy, assessing hepatic synthetic function (PT/INR is one of the most sensitive markers of acute liver failure — the liver synthesizes all vitamin K-dependent factors II, VII, IX, and X, and protein C and S), evaluating coagulopathy in DIC, and guiding pre-procedural risk assessment. In liver disease, INR elevation reflects the degree of hepatic synthetic failure — a MELD score (Model for End-Stage Liver Disease) incorporates INR as a key component. However, INR may paradoxically underestimate bleeding risk in cirrhosis because the liver also produces thrombin inhibitors that are not measured by standard INR. Vitamin K deficiency from malnutrition, malabsorption, prolonged antibiotic use (reducing gut flora production), or warfarin toxicity responds to vitamin K administration. For warfarin reversal: non-emergent (INR 5-10 without bleeding) — hold warfarin and give oral vitamin K 2.5-5mg; emergent reversal (active major bleeding) — 4-factor PCC (rapid, preferred over FFP due to smaller volume and faster action) plus vitamin K 10mg IV. Factor VII has the shortest half-life, so INR begins to fall first upon warfarin discontinuation, but full reversal requires 48-72 hours for all factor levels to normalize.

critical_high: >3x upper limit of normal (>480 U/L) — highly specific for acute pancreatitis
critical_action: Lipase >3x ULN with abdominal pain and nausea: diagnose acute pancreatitis; aggressive IV fluid resuscitation (Lactated Ringer's preferred, 250-500 mL/hr initially); NPO vs. early enteral feeding; pain management with IV opioids; identify etiology (gallstones via ultrasound, alcohol history, triglycerides); CT abdomen if severe or complications suspected.
high_indicates: Acute pancreatitis (most important cause — diagnostic at >3x ULN)
low_indicates: Chronic pancreatitis with exocrine insufficiency (burned-out pancreas)
content: Serum lipase is the preferred biomarker for diagnosing acute pancreatitis due to its superior specificity compared to amylase. Lipase rises within 4-8 hours of pancreatic injury, peaks at 24 hours, and remains elevated for 7-14 days — a longer diagnostic window than amylase (which normalizes within 3-5 days). A lipase above 3 times the upper limit of normal (typically >480 U/L) in the appropriate clinical context (epigastric pain radiating to the back, nausea, vomiting) is highly specific for acute pancreatitis (specificity approximately 90%). The diagnosis of acute pancreatitis requires at least 2 of 3 criteria: (1) characteristic abdominal pain, (2) serum lipase or amylase >3x ULN, and (3) confirmatory CT or MRI findings. Etiology assessment is critical: gallstone pancreatitis (RUQ ultrasound showing gallstones, dilated CBD, elevated bilirubin, ALT) is the most common cause in women, alcohol in men; hypertriglyceridemia above 1000 mg/dL is a third major cause. Severity stratification uses the Ranson criteria, BISAP score, or APACHE II score — CT with contrast (CTSI, CT Severity Index) is performed when severe pancreatitis, clinical deterioration, or complications (necrosis, abscess, pseudocyst) are suspected, typically after 48-72 hours. Treatment: aggressive IV fluid resuscitation with Lactated Ringer's (preferred over normal saline in WATERFALL trial — reduces SIRS), early enteral nutrition via nasojejunal tube within 24 hours in severe pancreatitis (superior to TPN), and ERCP within 24 hours if cholangitis or persistent biliary obstruction complicates gallstone pancreatitis. Lipase elevation in renal failure (reduced clearance) and macrolipasemia (benign enzyme-immunoglobulin complex) can cause false elevations without true pancreatic pathology.

critical_high: >10x ULN (>560 U/L) — acute hepatocellular injury; >1000 U/L — acute severe hepatitis (viral, ischemic, or toxic)
critical_action: ALT >10x ULN: evaluate for acute hepatitis (viral hepatitis A/B/C serologies, autoimmune hepatitis ANA/ASMA, acetaminophen toxicity, ischemic hepatitis); check PT/INR for synthetic function; hepatology consult. ALT >1000 U/L with rising INR: acute liver failure protocol — N-acetylcysteine, early transplant center evaluation.
high_indicates: Acute viral hepatitis (HAV, HBV, HCV, HEV)
Alcoholic hepatitis (AST:ALT ratio >2:1 in alcoholic liver disease)
Biliary obstruction (cholestatic pattern — ALT less elevated than in hepatocellular injury)
low_indicates: Severe malnutrition (pyridoxal phosphate deficiency can lower ALT)
Advanced cirrhosis (end-stage liver may not generate high ALT despite severe disease)
content: Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) is a cytoplasmic enzyme found predominantly in hepatocytes, making it the most liver-specific aminotransferase and the preferred marker for hepatocellular injury. Unlike AST (which is also found in cardiac muscle, skeletal muscle, and kidneys), ALT elevation strongly indicates liver pathology. Normal ALT is 7-56 U/L in men and 7-45 U/L in women — sex-specific thresholds reflect genuine sex differences in hepatocellular enzyme concentrations. ALT patterns guide diagnosis: Hepatocellular pattern (predominantly ALT and AST elevation with lesser ALP rise) suggests viral hepatitis, drug-induced liver injury, autoimmune hepatitis, ischemic hepatitis, or alcoholic hepatitis. The AST:ALT ratio is a key clinical clue: ratio above 2:1 strongly suggests alcoholic liver disease (alcohol preferentially induces mitochondrial AST release and vitamin B6 deficiency impairs ALT production), while ratio below 1 suggests viral or NAFLD/NASH. Ischemic hepatitis (shock liver) from cardiogenic shock or hypotension causes extreme transaminase elevations above 1000-10,000 U/L — often called the 'hepatic smash' — with rapid normalization when perfusion is restored. Acetaminophen toxicity causes the highest ALT values (often above 3,000-10,000 U/L) along with rising INR indicating acute liver failure, requiring immediate N-acetylcysteine. Cholestatic pattern (predominantly ALP and bilirubin elevation with mild transaminase rise) occurs in biliary obstruction, PSC, PBC, and drug-induced cholestasis. Albumin and PT/INR are the most important markers of hepatic synthetic function — while ALT reflects liver injury, falling albumin and rising INR indicate failing liver function. NAFLD is the most common cause of mild chronic ALT elevation in the developed world — defined by elevated ALT with fatty liver on imaging without other causes.

normal_range_pediatric: 0.7 - 6.4 mIU/L (newborn screening: 0-25 mIU/L normal in first week)
critical_high: >10 mIU/L (overt hypothyroidism requiring treatment); >20 mIU/L (possible myxedema coma in symptomatic patient)
critical_action: TSH <0.01 with free T4 >1.8: evaluate for Graves disease (TSI antibodies), toxic adenoma, toxic multinodular goiter; check for thyroid storm (fever, tachycardia, altered mental status, organ failure — treat with PTU/methimazole, propranolol, iodine, hydrocortisone). TSH >20 with hypothyroid symptoms: start levothyroxine; in elderly/cardiac patients start at 12.5-25 mcg/day.
high_indicates: TSH-secreting pituitary adenoma (with elevated T4 — rare)
low_indicates: Hyperthyroidism (Graves disease, toxic adenoma, toxic MNG)
Secondary hypothyroidism (pituitary failure — low TSH with low T4)
content: TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone) from the anterior pituitary is the most sensitive first-line test for thyroid dysfunction due to the inverse logarithmic relationship between TSH and free thyroid hormone levels — small changes in free T4 cause large proportional changes in TSH. A normal TSH reliably rules out primary thyroid disease in the vast majority of cases, making it the single best screening test. Elevated TSH (above 4.0 mIU/L) indicates primary hypothyroidism — the pituitary senses insufficient thyroid hormone and increases TSH secretion. The most common cause is Hashimoto thyroiditis (autoimmune — check anti-TPO antibodies). Subclinical hypothyroidism (TSH 4-10 mIU/L with normal free T4) may be treated based on symptoms, TSH level, and risk factors (pregnancy, significant coronary artery disease). Overt hypothyroidism (TSH >10 with low free T4) requires levothyroxine replacement in virtually all patients. A suppressed TSH (below 0.1 mIU/L) indicates hyperthyroidism — the pituitary is suppressed by excess thyroid hormone. Check free T4 and free T3 to distinguish overt hyperthyroidism (elevated free T4 or T3) from subclinical hyperthyroidism (suppressed TSH with normal free T4/T3). The most common cause is Graves disease (diffuse goiter, ophthalmopathy, elevated TSH receptor antibodies). Thyroid storm — a life-threatening thyrotoxic crisis — is a clinical diagnosis: fever, tachycardia/AF, tremor, altered mental status, and organ failure (GI, cardiac, CNS) in a patient with hyperthyroidism triggered by surgery, infection, or iodinated contrast. Treatment uses the four B's: Block synthesis (PTU preferred over methimazole in storm — also blocks T4→T3 conversion), Block release (iodine — Lugol's solution 1 hour after PTU), Beta-blocker (propranolol), and Betamethasone/steroids. TSH is unreliable in critical illness (sick euthyroid syndrome) and after recent changes in levothyroxine dose — allow 6-8 weeks for TSH to reflect new steady state.

normal_range_adult_male: 0.5 - 1.0 mmol/L (venous); up to 2.0 mmol/L acceptable in low-acuity settings
critical_high: >4.0 mmol/L (severe lactic acidosis — high mortality); >2.0 mmol/L meets sepsis-3 lactate criterion for septic shock
critical_action: Lactate >2.0 in suspected infection: diagnose septic shock if MAP <65 despite fluids — initiate Surviving Sepsis Bundle (fluids 30 mL/kg x1h, blood cultures x2 sets, broad-spectrum antibiotics, vasopressors, lactate repeat at 2h). Lactate >4.0: ICU admission, aggressive resuscitation, 2-hour lactate clearance goal (reduce by >10%). Persistent high lactate despite resuscitation: search for surgical source (ischemic bowel, necrotic source), consider thiamine administration (Wernicke/lactate block).
high_indicates: Septic shock (most common ICU cause — tissue hypoperfusion)
specimen: Arterial blood (gold standard) or venous blood on ice — must be processed within 15-30 minutes
content: Serum lactate is one of the most important biomarkers in critical care, serving as a marker of tissue hypoperfusion, metabolic crisis, and disease severity. It is the primary trigger and monitoring parameter in the Sepsis-3 definition and Surviving Sepsis Campaign guidelines. Lactate above 2 mmol/L in the setting of suspected infection and hypotension defines septic shock and mandates aggressive intervention per the hour-1 bundle: blood cultures, broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour, 30 mL/kg crystalloid IV bolus, and vasopressors if MAP remains below 65 mmHg. Lactate above 4 mmol/L indicates severe lactic acidosis with very high mortality and requires ICU-level resuscitation. Lactate clearance — the fall in lactate over 2-6 hours of resuscitation — is a more dynamic marker of response to therapy than a single value. Target greater than 10% lactate clearance per 2 hours (LACTATE trial), with normalization below 2 mmol/L within 6 hours as a resuscitation goal. Lactic acidosis is classified as Type A (tissue hypoperfusion — most common; shock, cardiac arrest, severe anemia, CO poisoning) or Type B (no obvious hypoperfusion; metformin accumulation, liver failure, malignancy, mitochondrial disease, thiamine deficiency, cyanide). Metformin-associated lactic acidosis requires hemodialysis to remove both metformin and lactate. Thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency blocks pyruvate dehydrogenase, forcing pyruvate to lactate — all patients with refractory lactic acidosis should receive empiric thiamine 200mg IV before glucose administration. Venous lactate is a reliable substitute for arterial lactate in most clinical situations (venous 0.5-1.5 mmol/L above arterial is acceptable). Specimen must be processed within 15-30 minutes without delay or on ice to prevent in-vitro glycolysis falsely elevating the result.

normal_range_pediatric: <0.1 ng/mL (neonates may have higher physiologic levels in first 48 hours of life)
critical_high: >10 ng/mL (severe bacterial sepsis or septic shock — very high specificity)
critical_action: Procalcitonin >2.0 with clinical sepsis: continue empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics; blood cultures; source control evaluation. Procalcitonin trending downward with clinical improvement: consider antibiotic de-escalation or discontinuation (target <0.25 ng/mL or >80% decrease from peak for antibiotic stewardship). Procalcitonin >10: bacterial sepsis/shock likely — escalate antibiotics, ICU evaluation.
high_indicates: Bacterial sepsis (highly sensitive and specific for systemic bacterial infection)
low_indicates: Viral infections (PCT typically normal or minimally elevated — useful for antibiotic stewardship)
Localized infections (uncomplicated UTI, cellulitis — PCT often normal)
content: Procalcitonin (PCT) is a propeptide of calcitonin produced primarily by hepatocytes and monocytes in response to bacterial infections and pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-alpha, IL-6), but suppressed by viral infections and interferon-gamma. This differential response makes PCT the most clinically useful biomarker for distinguishing bacterial from viral etiologies of infection and inflammation, enabling antibiotic stewardship. PCT rises rapidly within 2-4 hours of bacterial infection (compared to 24-48 hours for CRP) and parallels disease severity — values above 0.5 ng/mL suggest bacterial infection requiring antibiotics, above 2.0 ng/mL indicates systemic bacterial infection (sepsis), and above 10 ng/mL is highly specific for severe bacterial sepsis or septic shock. Serial PCT measurements are the most validated application: PCT-guided antibiotic de-escalation protocols consistently reduce antibiotic duration by 2-3 days without adverse outcomes across multiple disease states including CAP, COPD exacerbation, sepsis, and ICU infections (PROACT, STOP-IT, PASS trials). The PCT-guided decision rule: antibiotics can be safely discontinued when PCT falls below 0.25 ng/mL or declines by more than 80% from peak value. PCT has lower diagnostic utility in: localized infections where systemic spillover is minimal (uncomplicated UTI, cellulitis, wound infections); CKD (reduced renal clearance raises baseline); post-surgical or post-trauma states (physiologic PCT rise without infection for 48-72 hours); neonatal physiology (higher baseline in first 48 hours of life). Medullary thyroid carcinoma produces calcitonin/PCT as a tumor marker (unrelated to infection). In COVID-19, PCT is typically low — a rising PCT in COVID-19 suggests secondary bacterial superinfection.

units: Multiple: pH (dimensionless), PaCO2 (mmHg), PaO2 (mmHg), HCO3- (mEq/L), Base Excess (mEq/L), SaO2 (%)
normal_range_adult_male: pH 7.35-7.45; PaCO2 35-45 mmHg; PaO2 75-100 mmHg; HCO3- 22-26 mEq/L; BE -2 to +2; SaO2 >95%
normal_range_adult_female: pH 7.35-7.45; PaCO2 35-45 mmHg; PaO2 75-100 mmHg; HCO3- 22-26 mEq/L; BE -2 to +2; SaO2 >95%
normal_range_pediatric: pH 7.35-7.45; PaCO2 35-45 mmHg; PaO2 75-100 mmHg; HCO3- 20-26 mEq/L
critical_low: pH <7.20 (severe acidosis — cardiac arrhythmia and hemodynamic instability risk); PaO2 <55 mmHg (hypoxemic respiratory failure)
critical_high: pH >7.60 (severe alkalosis — neuromuscular excitability, arrhythmia); PaCO2 >70 mmHg (acute hypercapnic respiratory failure — impending intubation)
critical_action: pH <7.20: identify primary disorder and treat underlying cause; consider sodium bicarbonate if metabolic acidosis pH <7.1 with hemodynamic instability; ventilatory support if respiratory acidosis with fatigue. PaO2 <55 or SaO2 <88%: supplemental oxygen; NIV (CPAP/BiPAP) for COPD or HF; mechanical ventilation if refractory. PaCO2 >70 with altered mental status: intubation or NIV.
high_indicates: High PaCO2: hypoventilation (COPD exacerbation, neuromuscular disease, sedation, obesity hypoventilation syndrome)
High pH (alkalosis): metabolic alkalosis (vomiting, diuretics) or respiratory alkalosis (hyperventilation, anxiety, PE, sepsis early)
low_indicates: Low pH (acidosis): metabolic acidosis (anion gap — MUDPILES: methanol, uremia, DKA, propylene glycol, isoniazid, lactic acidosis, ethylene glycol, salicylates) or respiratory acidosis (hypoventilation). Low PaCO2: hyperventilation (anxiety, PE, sepsis, liver failure)
related_tests: Serum osmolality (osmolar gap in toxin screen)
specimen: Arterial blood (heparinized syringe; process immediately on ice)
content: Arterial blood gas analysis provides comprehensive real-time assessment of acid-base status, ventilation (PaCO2), and oxygenation (PaO2, SaO2). Systematic ABG interpretation follows a structured approach: Step 1 — assess pH (normal 7.35-7.45; <7.35 = acidosis; >7.45 = alkalosis). Step 2 — identify the primary disorder by examining PaCO2 (respiratory) and HCO3- (metabolic). Step 3 — assess compensation (respiratory or metabolic compensates for the primary disorder, never fully normalizing pH). Step 4 — calculate anion gap (Na - [Cl + HCO3-]; normal 8-12 mEq/L) if metabolic acidosis; elevated anion gap > 12 = MUDPILES mnemonic (Methanol, Uremia, DKA, Propylene glycol, Isoniazid, Lactic acidosis, Ethylene glycol, Salicylates). Step 5 — if elevated anion gap, calculate delta-delta ratio to detect concurrent metabolic alkalosis or normal anion gap acidosis. Respiratory acidosis (elevated PaCO2, low pH): acute — CNS depression, neuromuscular failure, severe asthma, COPD exacerbation; chronic — COPD, obesity hypoventilation, chronic neuromuscular disease (with compensatory metabolic alkalosis — elevated HCO3-). Respiratory alkalosis (low PaCO2, elevated pH): PE, sepsis (early), anxiety, pregnancy, hepatic failure, high altitude. Metabolic alkalosis (elevated HCO3-): vomiting (HCl loss), diuretics, hypokalemia, Bartter/Gitelman syndrome. Oxygenation: PaO2/FiO2 ratio (P/F ratio) is used to classify ARDS (P/F <300 = mild, <200 = moderate, <100 = severe). Hypoxemic respiratory failure (PaO2 <60 mmHg on room air) requires supplemental oxygen; hypercapnic respiratory failure (PaCO2 >50 with acidosis) may require NIV or mechanical ventilation. In COPD, a chronically elevated PaCO2 is expected — use HCO3- and pH to determine if the current presentation is acute-on-chronic or fully compensated.

critical_high: >10 mg/dL (with risk of gout attack or urate nephropathy)
critical_action: Uric acid >10 in tumor lysis syndrome: IV fluids (aggressive hydration), rasburicase (recombinant uricase — rapidly reduces urate) or allopurinol; monitor renal function and electrolytes (potassium, phosphate, calcium) closely. Uric acid >7 in known gout: initiate urate-lowering therapy (allopurinol or febuxostat after acute flare resolves); target serum uric acid <6 mg/dL.
high_indicates: Gout (hyperuricemia — necessary but not sufficient for gout diagnosis)
Tumor lysis syndrome (massive purine release from lysed cancer cells)
Diuretic use (thiazides and loop diuretics reduce renal urate excretion)
High purine diet (red meat, organ meats, shellfish, fructose)
low_indicates: Medications (losartan — uricosuric effect; probenecid; SGLT2 inhibitors)
Wilson disease (defective copper transport impairs xanthine oxidase)
related_tests: 24-hour urine uric acid (under-excreter vs. over-producer evaluation)
Synovial fluid analysis (MSU crystals — definitive gout diagnosis)
LDH and potassium (tumor lysis syndrome monitoring)
content: Serum uric acid is the end product of purine metabolism, produced when xanthine oxidase converts xanthine and hypoxanthine to uric acid. In humans (who lack uricase enzyme), uric acid is excreted by the kidneys and intestines. Hyperuricemia (above 6.8 mg/dL — the saturation threshold at body temperature) is the prerequisite for gout but is not sufficient alone — most hyperuricemic individuals never develop gout. Gout is diagnosed clinically and confirmed by demonstrating monosodium urate (MSU) crystals in synovial fluid by polarized microscopy (needle-shaped, negatively birefringent crystals). Serum uric acid may be normal or low during an acute gout flare (inflammatory cytokines lower urate levels transiently) — normal serum uric acid does not exclude gout. Urate-lowering therapy (allopurinol, febuxostat) targets serum uric acid below 6 mg/dL (below 5 mg/dL if tophi are present) and must never be initiated during an acute flare (mobilization effect can prolong the attack). Colchicine or NSAID prophylaxis covers the first 3-6 months of urate-lowering therapy. Tumor lysis syndrome (TLS) — a metabolic emergency occurring after chemotherapy for rapidly proliferating cancers (Burkitt lymphoma, AML) — causes massive release of intracellular contents: hyperuricemia, hyperphosphatemia, hypocalcemia, hyperkalemia, and AKI from urate crystal nephropathy. Rasburicase (recombinant uricase) is the most effective treatment for established TLS, rapidly converting urate to allantoin (the soluble form excreted by humans). Rasburicase is contraindicated in G6PD deficiency (causes oxidative hemolysis).

critical_high: >15 mg/dL (severe inflammation or infection)
critical_action: CRP >15 mg/dL with fever: evaluate for severe infection or sepsis; consider blood cultures, procalcitonin, and initiate empiric antibiotics if clinically indicated. CRP tracking: rising CRP despite treatment indicates inadequate source control or resistant organism; declining CRP with clinical improvement supports antibiotic de-escalation. CRP >50 mg/dL with fever and arthritis in child: evaluate for systemic JIA (Still disease requires very high CRP).
high_indicates: Acute MI (rises after 6-12 hours — marker of inflammation not necrosis)
low_indicates: Note: SLE often has normal or minimally elevated CRP despite active disease — unless serositis or concurrent infection
Viral infections (CRP mildly elevated unlike marked PCT elevation in bacterial infection)
content: C-reactive protein (CRP) is an acute-phase protein produced by the liver in response to IL-6 and other pro-inflammatory cytokines within 6-12 hours of tissue injury or infection. CRP rises and falls more rapidly than ESR (which may lag by days), making it more useful for monitoring acute inflammatory processes and treatment response. Normal CRP is below 1.0 mg/dL (<10 mg/L). High-sensitivity CRP (hsCRP), measuring CRP at lower concentrations, is used for cardiovascular risk stratification — hsCRP above 2 mg/L is associated with increased cardiovascular event risk independent of LDL cholesterol. CRP is highly non-specific — any cause of inflammation (infection, autoimmune disease, malignancy, trauma, surgery, acute MI) elevates it. However, the magnitude of elevation can guide diagnosis: CRP above 150-200 mg/L (15-20 mg/dL) is typical of severe bacterial infection, sepsis, or major tissue necrosis; CRP of 50-150 mg/L occurs with moderate bacterial infection, autoimmune flares, or vasculitis; CRP of 10-50 mg/L is seen with mild-moderate infection, viral illness, or chronic inflammatory disease. A critical diagnostic pearl: SLE typically has NORMAL or only mildly elevated CRP despite severe disease activity because IFN-alpha (elevated in SLE) suppresses hepatic CRP production. A patient with known SLE presenting with markedly elevated CRP above 60 mg/L should be evaluated for infection or serositis rather than attributed to SLE flare alone. Conversely, rheumatoid arthritis, vasculitis, and adult Still disease characteristically cause very high CRP elevations proportional to disease activity — CRP is a reliable measure of RA disease activity and response to therapy (target CRP normalization). For monitoring, serial CRP measurements are more valuable than a single value.

critical_high: >13.0 mg/dL (cardiac arrhythmias, coma risk)
critical_action: Critical low calcium <7.0 with tetany/seizures/laryngospasm: IV calcium gluconate 1-2g over 10-20 minutes; cardiac monitoring; identify cause (hypoparathyroidism, vitamin D deficiency, pancreatitis, hyperphosphatemia). Critical high >13.0: aggressive IV saline hydration 200-300 mL/hr (first priority — expand volume); furosemide once adequately hydrated (promotes calciuresis); calcitonin 4 IU/kg SC/IM q12h (rapid onset, tachyphylaxis after 48h); bisphosphonates (pamidronate or zoledronic acid — delayed onset 48-72h but sustained); dialysis for refractory or renal failure.
high_indicates: Primary hyperparathyroidism (most common outpatient cause — elevated PTH with hypercalcemia)
Malignancy-associated hypercalcemia (PTHrP from lung/breast/renal cancers; osteolytic bone mets from multiple myeloma)
Sarcoidosis and other granulomatous diseases (1-alpha hydroxylase in macrophages)
Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia (FHH — benign, urine Ca/Cr <0.01)
low_indicates: CKD (impaired 1,25-OH2D synthesis and phosphate retention causing hypocalcemia)
Acute pancreatitis (saponification — fatty acid binding of calcium)
related_tests: Albumin (correct for hypoalbuminemia: corrected Ca = total Ca + 0.8 × (4 - albumin g/dL))
ECG (prolonged QTc in hypocalcemia; shortened QTc in hypercalcemia)
content: Serum total calcium reflects the sum of three fractions: protein-bound calcium (approximately 45%, primarily to albumin), complexed calcium (10%, bound to citrate, phosphate), and ionized/free calcium (45%, the biologically active form). Because albumin binding affects measured total calcium, hypoalbuminemia falsely lowers total calcium — use the corrected calcium formula: add 0.8 mg/dL for each 1 g/dL that albumin is below 4 g/dL. Ionized calcium measurement directly assesses the active fraction and is preferred in critically ill patients with altered albumin levels. Hypercalcemia workup: check PTH first. Elevated PTH with hypercalcemia = primary hyperparathyroidism (most common, usually from solitary adenoma — parathyroidectomy is curative). Suppressed PTH with hypercalcemia = PTHrP-mediated malignancy (squamous cell carcinoma of lung, renal cell, breast), metastatic bone disease (multiple myeloma causes lytic lesions and hypercalcemia from osteoclast activation without PTHrP), or vitamin D toxicity (check 25-OH vitamin D and 1,25-OH2D). Granulomatous diseases (sarcoidosis, TB, histoplasmosis) cause hypercalcemia through autonomous macrophage 1-alpha hydroxylase activity. The mnemonic for hypercalcemia causes: Bones (hyperparathyroidism, bone mets), Stones (nephrolithiasis), Groans (GI symptoms), and Psychic moans (cognitive dysfunction). Hypocalcemia symptoms include neuromuscular excitability — Chvostek sign (facial twitch with cheek tap), Trousseau sign (carpal spasm with BP cuff inflation), perioral numbness, and tetany. Long-standing hypocalcemia causes cataracts and basal ganglia calcifications. ECG changes are diagnostically important: hypocalcemia prolongs QTc (risk of torsades); hypercalcemia shortens QTc and can cause bradyarrhythmias.

critical_high: >4.9 mg/dL (toxicity — loss of deep tendon reflexes, respiratory failure risk)
critical_action: Severe hypomagnesemia <1.0 or symptomatic: IV magnesium sulfate 2-4g over 4-6 hours; repeat serum Mg and replete before potassium (refractory hypokalemia will not correct until Mg is repleted); ECG monitoring. Hypermagnesemia >4.9 (usually iatrogenic — eclampsia treatment): IV calcium gluconate 1g over 5-10 minutes (physiologic antagonist); stop magnesium infusion; supportive care; dialysis if severe renal failure.
high_indicates: Renal failure (most common — reduced magnesium excretion)
Excessive antacid or laxative use (magnesium-containing products)
low_indicates: Alcohol use disorder (poor intake + increased renal wasting)
Diarrhea and other GI losses (malabsorption, short bowel)
Diuretic use (loop diuretics increase Mg excretion)
PPI use long-term (impairs intestinal Mg absorption)
Diabetic ketoacidosis during treatment (insulin drives Mg into cells)
Refeeding syndrome (cellular Mg uptake during anabolism)
Cisplatin (direct renal tubular toxicity — magnesium wasting nephropathy)
related_tests: Serum potassium (concurrent hypokalemia is very common — both require repletion)
Serum calcium (hypomagnesemia impairs PTH release and action — hypocalcemia)
ECG (prolonged PR, widened QRS in toxicity; U-waves and torsades risk in deficiency)
24-hour urine magnesium (to distinguish renal vs. GI wasting)
content: Serum magnesium is the fourth most abundant cation in the body and the second most abundant intracellular cation, yet hypomagnesemia is the most common electrolyte abnormality in hospitalized patients — and often unrecognized. Magnesium is critical for over 300 enzymatic reactions, neuromuscular transmission, and cardiac electrophysiology. Hypomagnesemia (below 1.7 mg/dL) causes its most clinically significant effects through interactions with other electrolytes: it impairs PTH secretion and peripheral PTH action, causing hypocalcemia refractory to calcium supplementation until magnesium is repleted; it also impairs renal potassium retention through effects on ROMK channels, causing hypokalemia refractory to potassium supplementation. The clinical rule: always replete magnesium before or alongside potassium and calcium in deficient patients. Magnesium depletion causes neuromuscular excitability (tremor, tetany, seizures), cardiac arrhythmias (torsades de pointes — magnesium is the treatment of choice), and hypokalemia with weakness. Long-term PPI use is a clinically important but frequently overlooked cause of hypomagnesemia — magnesium absorption in the intestine depends on TRPM6/7 channels regulated by gastric acid; PPIs reduce this absorption and can cause severe symptomatic hypomagnesemia after months to years of use. IV magnesium sulfate is both the treatment for eclampsia (seizure prophylaxis and treatment in pre-eclampsia) and the treatment for torsades de pointes (2g IV push over 15 minutes). In preeclampsia, magnesium toxicity monitoring is essential: loss of patellar reflexes (Mg 7-10 mg/dL) is the earliest sign, followed by respiratory depression (Mg >12 mg/dL) and cardiac arrest. Calcium gluconate 1g IV is the antidote for magnesium toxicity.
